What's the best value in a good $200-$300 camcorder with great optical zoom, true HD, and good low-light performance?

I want it all and I want it cheap. Sorry you're not going to combine all those things in a $300 camcorder. In fact good low light performance and great zoom don't really go together. The reason is low light performance is typically achieved by using a bigger sensor and that makes a zoom lens bigger too, the other way is to use a lens with a fast constant aperture. Both of these ways means a much higher price tag. Also you "True HD" is a marketing term. Are you wanting 1080p vs 1080i, a specific file output? If you want to ask more specific questions please do but please remember the is no perfect video camera and if by some miracle some company made one I'd be really expensive. General advice would be to forget about anything that's considered good in low light by industry standards and buy a Sony or Canon in your price range.

I'd mainly like to get something weighted toward the features mentioned (because those would be most useful) and I think it's possible within the $200-$300 price range to beat out my old Sony DTR-TRV30 which sold for about $1500 new.

As someone who hasn't been closely monitoring the advances since 2003 when I bought my first and only camcorder, I figured you folks might at least point me to some devices that are more on the winner side of this feature set than the loser side.

My family tends to get a lot of Nikons and some have suggested maybe even getting a camera compatible with those lenses, but most of these lack a lot of ports and features common with camcorders.

As for the Sony... the one I had was an astoundingly stupid design, IMHO. It was essentially several different devices crammed in one case with a selector switch that only allowed you to use one at a time, and an annoying reboot sequence any time you flipped the switch. I really hope they've done away with "Memory Mode", "VCR Mode", and "Still Camera Mode". Also frustrating to me was that you had to move images from Memory in Memory Mode via USB, but to move video content you had to switch to VCR mode and use FireWire.

As a Computer Engineer, I understand the challenges of integrating the separate systems, and maybe most people didn't mind, but I'd like to be able to do things like snap a still image while recording video (which my current camera kind of allows by recording the still image across 3 seconds of MiniDV tape) - and it wasn't really easy to get that into a JPG. It was also annoying to have to switch to a much slower data transfer technology... just because I took a few pics on my Memory Stick.

As for the HD question, I was thinking 1080p.

Wow. TRV30 takes me back. So every thing now is better and if that's your base idea of what you want to be better then you're in luck.

First lets talk about the Nikon lenses. What you would be buying is a Nikon DSLR, not a video camera. The difference is that the DSLR will not shoot more than 30 continuous minutes of video. It will also likely cost more than $300 for a current new unit. You could probably buy used or old stock for $300. The sensor size in the Nikon is larger than most video cameras so it good in low light. Interchangeable lenses means lots of options but also more money and more space is used.

Second all consumer video cameras will have a still more and video mode on them. Some will let you snap a still while taking video so if that's super important you'll need to seek that feature specifically while looking. (Side note: at 1080p if you pull a still frame out of the video with software you are generally left with a 2 megapixel jpg file that's fine for a screen or a 4x6" hard copy). As far as memory and vcr modes go they are non existent anymore since all media is recorded to flash memory. Usually an SD card, but there are others out there.

Third is cables. More good news. Your video camera will come with the download or transfer cable. It will be USB on one end for the computer and most likely micro USB on the end for the camera. This will transfer all media on your video camera. Since they all pretty much us SD cards you could even just stick it in the card reader that's probably in you computer. For direct play back on an HD TV you will need a mini-HDMI to HDMI cable. Some video cameras come with them some don't. I never could tell why some models came with them while some did not.

Finally we get to files. This is mixed news. The good part is any stills you snap will be easy to handle jpgs. The bad news is HD video files can be difficult. So you have the 3 big file types currently used for most video; XAVC, MPEG4 and AVCHD. XAVC is mainly used by pros and enthusiasts and probably not available at a $300 price point. MPEG 4 is used by most devices and is the closest thing to a "universal" format. AVCHD is better quality than MPEG 4 but is a Sony thing and thus kind of a pain. As for 1080p just double check while you're looking. Most things are 1080p now but occasionally some one tries to slip in 1080i.

Hope this helps and coming off a TRV30 I'm sure you can find what you're looking for in a Canon or Sony at your price point.
